title: Five Explanations, All of Them Fit
scopeNote: This keeps the case, the competing explanations, the evidence requests and the live recomputation of where each account stands, cut to five explanations and four pieces of evidence. The rating stage, the confidence scoring, the compatibility map and three further explanations stay in the longer version.
summary: Five accounts of why one fictional person volunteered, all of which fit. Request the evidence, watch two fall, and notice that one of the survivors survived by never committing itself to anything.
learningObjectives: Distinguish an explanation that fits from one that predicts.
Explain why an account that accommodates every detail is weaker rather than stronger.
Say what evidence would choose between two accounts that both fit.
Distinguish surviving the evidence from being supported by it.
Recognise underdetermination as the ordinary situation rather than a failure.
Recognise that compatible explanations do not compete.
interactionTypes: a judgement about what makes one explanation better than another
evidence requested one piece at a time
each account's standing recomputed as evidence arrives
a count of how much each account committed itself to
a piece of deciding evidence that is visibly unavailable
a guided route that requests everything available
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. The learner is not asked about themselves or about anybody they know.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Evidence requests are ordinary buttons, and a requested one is marked with aria-disabled rather than the disabled attribute so it stays reachable and readable. Every account's standing is in a real table with row and column headers and is stated in words, with the reason for a fall spelled out rather than signalled by colour; rows also carry a non-colour state attribute. The findings appear as text notices, so nothing depends on a figure. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Priya is fictional and her behaviour was written to be compatible with every account offered. Each account's predictions were also written in advance rather than derived, and nothing here is evidence about any real person.
simulationNotes: Each explanation records what it predicts about each piece of evidence as plus one, minus one or nothing, and each piece of evidence has the direction it actually came out. An explanation is contradicted if it predicted the opposite of the finding, supported if it predicted the finding, and untouched if it predicted nothing. Its risk is the count of requested pieces it committed itself on, and that count is what the activity is for. The five accounts and three available pieces were arranged so that no single piece settles the case, each piece rules out at least one account, exactly two accounts fall once all three are in, and the three survivors differ sharply in what they staked: three commitments for the achievement account, two for self-efficacy and one for the broad trait. The fourth piece of evidence, what she does in a different setting over the following months, cannot be requested, and it is the only thing that separates the survivors: the trait and achievement accounts predict the behaviour generalises and the self-efficacy account, being domain-specific by definition, predicts it does not. It is shown from the beginning rather than held back, because the deciding observation being unavailable is the ordinary condition and not a twist. Simplifications: predictions are supplied rather than derived, which is the part real life does not do; evidence points cleanly one way, where real evidence is mixed; and some accounts here are compatible rather than competing, which the page states and the longer version maps explicitly.
readmeTopic: why an explanation that fits everything has told you nothing
